entries.meaning: Small, delicate and pretty. ---
examples: She wore dainty gold earrings.
They served dainty little sandwiches with the tea.
Her handwriting was daintier than mine.

entries.meaning: Damaged has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The package arrived damaged.
The storm left dozens of damaged homes.
The most damaged buildings were near the coast.
He was a damaged kid from a violent home.
She seemed deeply damaged by the divorce.

senses.head: Harmed or broken, so it no longer works or looks as it should
examples: The package arrived damaged.
The storm left dozens of damaged homes.
The most damaged buildings were near the coast.

senses.head: Emotionally hurt by bad experiences in the past
examples: He was a damaged kid from a violent home.
She seemed deeply damaged by the divorce.

entries.meaning: Causing harm or damage. ---
examples: The scandal was damaging to her career.
Too much sun can have damaging effects on your skin.
The most damaging evidence came from his own emails.
entries.form: -ing from damage — what causes the damage

entries.meaning: Used before a noun to show anger or annoyance, or just for emphasis. ---
examples: The damn car won't start again.
Turn off that damn TV!
It's a damn shame they closed the old diner.
entries.contrast: A mild swear word: fine among friends, not in a job interview. Damn is also an adverb (damn good), an interjection (Damn!) and a noun (I don't give a damn). Damned means the same before a noun; darn is the polite version.

entries.meaning: Damned has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The damned printer is jammed again.
I can't find my damned phone.
It was the damnedest thing — the dog opened the door by itself.
They believed the souls of sinners were damned forever.
You're damned if you do and damned if you don't.

senses.head: Used before a noun to show anger or annoyance, or just for emphasis
examples: The damned printer is jammed again.
I can't find my damned phone.
It was the damnedest thing — the dog opened the door by itself.

senses.head: Condemned to hell, or certain to fail whatever you do
examples: They believed the souls of sinners were damned forever.
You're damned if you do and damned if you don't.

entries.comparison: not gradable — except the idiom damnedest (the damnedest thing = the strangest)
entries.contrast: Stronger than darned, about as strong as damn. The damned (noun) are the souls in hell. I'll be damned! shows surprise; I'll be damned if I pay that means I refuse to. Damned good is the adverb.

entries.meaning: Showing clearly that someone has done something wrong. ---
examples: The report contains damning evidence against the company.
The video was damning.
The most damning testimony came from his former assistant.

entries.meaning: Slightly wet, often in an unpleasant way. ---
examples: Wipe the table with a damp cloth.
The basement always feels cold and damp.
My towel was even damper the next morning.
entries.contrast: Russian влажный has three English partners: damp (a little wet, often unpleasant: a damp basement), moist (pleasantly: moist cake) and humid (air and weather).

entries.meaning: Of music, with a rhythm that is good for dancing. ---
examples: The band plays upbeat, danceable music.
The song is catchy and danceable.
Her new album is more danceable than the last one.

entries.meaning: Very good; often used ironically to mean the opposite. ---
examples: Everything is fine and dandy here.
We missed the flight? Well, that's just dandy.
Grandpa thought it was a dandy idea.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb, in fine and dandy and just dandy
entries.contrast: Old-fashioned and often ironic today: Oh, that's just dandy means that's terrible. A dandy (noun) is a man who cares a lot about his clothes.

entries.meaning: Likely to cause harm, injury or death. ---
examples: It's dangerous to swim here after dark.
Smoking is dangerous to your health.
This is the most dangerous road in the state.

entries.meaning: Unpleasantly cold, wet and smelling of mold. ---
examples: The prisoners were kept in a dank cell.
The cabin smelled dank after the rainy winter.
The basement was the dankest room in the house.
entries.contrast: In slang, dank means excellent (dank memes); it is informal and mostly online.

entries.meaning: Of a man, neat, well-dressed and stylish. ---
examples: He looked dapper in his navy suit.
A dapper old man tipped his hat to us.
You look even more dapper with the beard.

entries.meaning: Marked with patches of light and shade, or with spots of color. ---
examples: We walked through the dappled shade of the forest.
She rode a dappled gray horse.
The garden was dappled with sunlight.

entries.meaning: Recklessly bold, taking dangerous risks for the thrill. ---
examples: He made his name with daredevil stunts on a motorcycle.
Her daredevil driving scares everyone in the car.
The show ended with a daredevil jump over eight buses.
entries.contrast: Much more common as a noun: The kid is a little daredevil.

entries.meaning: Daring has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Firefighters made a daring rescue from the roof.
She's more daring than her brother.
It was a daring plan, and it worked.
The designer showed some daring outfits.
The film was considered daring for its time.

senses.head: Brave and willing to take risks
examples: Firefighters made a daring rescue from the roof.
She's more daring than her brother.
It was a daring plan, and it worked.

senses.head: New or shocking, and likely to upset some people
examples: The designer showed some daring outfits.
The film was considered daring for its time.

entries.meaning: Having dark hair. ---
examples: A tall, dark-haired woman opened the door.
Both of their kids are dark-haired.
They're looking for a dark-haired actor to play the son.

entries.meaning: Having dark skin. ---
examples: Her father was dark-skinned and had curly hair.
The makeup brand offers shades for dark-skinned women.
Darker-skinned people can still get sunburned.

entries.meaning: Made dark, or with the lights turned off. ---
examples: We sat in the darkened theater waiting for the movie.
She walked down the darkened hallway.
The house stood darkened and silent.

entries.meaning: Darling has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She dedicated the book to her darling husband.
Our darling daughter turns five today.
What a darling little dress!
Isn't that cottage just darling?
It's the most darling shop in town.

senses.head: Much loved
examples: She dedicated the book to her darling husband.
Our darling daughter turns five today.

senses.head: Very pretty or charming
examples: What a darling little dress!
Isn't that cottage just darling?
It's the most darling shop in town.

entries.contrast: Mostly a noun used to address someone (Thanks, darling). As an adjective it sounds a little old-fashioned or gushing.

entries.meaning: Used to show annoyance or surprise, or just for emphasis, without swearing. ---
examples: The darned dog got out again.
Well, I'll be darned — you were right.
Kids say the darnedest things.
entries.comparison: not gradable — except the idiom darnedest (the darnedest things)
entries.contrast: A polite American way to avoid damned. Darned good is the adverb. Darned socks are mended ones, from the verb darn.

entries.meaning: Darwinian has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The course covers Darwinian evolution.
He explained the idea in Darwinian terms.
Silicon Valley can be a Darwinian place.
The airline industry is Darwinian: the weak go bankrupt.

senses.head: Relating to Charles Darwin or his theory of evolution
examples: The course covers Darwinian evolution.
He explained the idea in Darwinian terms.

senses.head: Brutally competitive, so that only the strongest survive
examples: Silicon Valley can be a Darwinian place.
The airline industry is Darwinian: the weak go bankrupt.

entries.comparison: not gradable — except sense 2: more Darwinian

entries.meaning: Attractive and stylish in a confident, exciting way, usually said of a man. ---
examples: A dashing young officer asked her to dance.
He looked dashing in his tuxedo.
He was the most dashing man at the party.

entries.meaning: Evil and cruel in a cowardly way. ---
examples: It was a dastardly attack on innocent people.
The cartoon villain twirled his mustache and made dastardly plans.
He's the most dastardly character in the book.
entries.contrast: Old-fashioned and now often humorous (a dastardly plot). It ends in -ly but is an adjective.

entries.meaning: Old-fashioned, belonging to an earlier time. ---
examples: The kitchen looks a little dated.
Some of the jokes in the movie feel dated now.
Of all the rooms, the bathroom looked the most dated.
entries.contrast: Not датированный: in a letter dated May 5, dated is the verb date. The adjective means old-fashioned.

entries.meaning: Seeming difficult or frightening, so that you lose confidence. ---
examples: Moving to a new country can be daunting.
She faced the daunting task of rebuilding the company.
The most daunting part was speaking in front of 500 people.
entries.form: -ing from daunt — what makes you lose confidence

entries.meaning: One day old; of food, not fresh because it was made the day before. ---
examples: The bakery sells day-old bread at half price.
The farm sells day-old chicks in the spring.
I'm not drinking day-old coffee.

entries.meaning: Happening every day as part of normal life or work. ---
examples: She handles the day-to-day running of the office.
Stress is part of my day-to-day life.
The manager deals with day-to-day problems.
entries.contrast: Hyphenated before a noun. Without hyphens it is usually an adverb phrase: We live day to day.

entries.meaning: Lasting all day. ---
examples: The museum is hosting a daylong festival.
Teachers attended a daylong training session.
After a daylong search, they found the missing hiker.

entries.meaning: Unable to think clearly, because of a blow, a shock or tiredness. ---
examples: He looked dazed after hitting his head.
Survivors wandered the streets, dazed and confused.
She walked out of the meeting with a dazed expression.

entries.meaning: Dazzling has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The dazzling sun reflected off the snow.
The lights on stage were dazzling.
She gave a dazzling performance.
The team's dazzling play won the crowd over.
It was the most dazzling smile I'd ever seen.

senses.head: So bright that you cannot see well for a moment
examples: The dazzling sun reflected off the snow.
The lights on stage were dazzling.

senses.head: Extremely impressive or beautiful
examples: She gave a dazzling performance.
The team's dazzling play won the crowd over.
It was the most dazzling smile I'd ever seen.

entries.meaning: Existing in fact, even if not officially or legally. ---
examples: English is the de facto language of international business.
He became the de facto leader of the group.
The river is now the de facto border between the two regions.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb: The country is de facto split in two.

entries.meaning: Existing by law or officially. ---
examples: The South had de jure segregation until the 1960s.
The country won de jure independence in 1991.
His power was de jure, but his deputy made the real decisions.

entries.meaning: Required by fashion, custom or good manners. ---
examples: A black tie is de rigueur at the gala.
Hoodies and sneakers are de rigueur in tech offices.
For a while, the man bun was a de rigueur look in Brooklyn.

entries.meaning: Dead set has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My parents were dead set against the move.
The mayor is dead set against raising taxes.
She's dead set on going to law school.
He was dead set on buying that truck.

senses.head: Completely opposed to something
examples: My parents were dead set against the move.
The mayor is dead set against raising taxes.

senses.head: Completely determined to do or get something
examples: She's dead set on going to law school.
He was dead set on buying that truck.

entries.takes: against + noun or -ing; on + noun or -ing
entries.contrast: The preposition changes the meaning: dead set against = strongly opposed; dead set on = determined to do or get it.

entries.meaning: Dead-end has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was stuck in a dead-end job.
She finally left her dead-end relationship.
We live on a quiet dead-end street.
The dead-end road stops at the river.

senses.head: Offering no chance of progress or a better future
examples: He was stuck in a dead-end job.
She finally left her dead-end relationship.

senses.head: Of a street, closed at one end
examples: We live on a quiet dead-end street.
The dead-end road stops at the river.

entries.contrast: The noun is two words with no hyphen: The road is a dead end.

entries.meaning: Exactly right. ---
examples: Your impression of the boss is dead-on.
Her prediction turned out to be dead-on.
He gave a dead-on description of the suspect.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb, usually without the hyphen: The clock is dead on time.

entries.meaning: Unable to reach an agreement or a decision. ---
examples: The jury was deadlocked after three days.
Talks between the union and the company remain deadlocked.
The deadlocked Senate could not pass the budget.

entries.meaning: Funny while showing no emotion and looking completely serious. ---
examples: He has a deadpan sense of humor.
Her delivery was completely deadpan.
His deadpan expression made the joke even funnier.
entries.form: compound — dead + pan (old slang for face)
entries.contrast: Also an adverb: She said it deadpan.

entries.meaning: Extremely loud. ---
examples: The music at the club was deafening.
There was a deafening explosion.
When he finished speaking, the silence was deafening.
entries.form: -ing from deafen — what makes you (almost) deaf

entries.meaning: Dear has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She's a dear friend of mine.
The house was very dear to him.
My dearest wish is to see my family again.
Dear Mr. Johnson, thank you for your letter.
She began the email with Dear Team.
Your grandmother is such a dear woman.
The Hendersons are dear people.

senses.head: Loved very much, or very important to someone
examples: She's a dear friend of mine.
The house was very dear to him.
My dearest wish is to see my family again.

senses.head: Used before a name or title at the start of a letter or email
examples: Dear Mr. Johnson, thank you for your letter.
She began the email with Dear Team.

senses.head: Sweet and kind; a little old-fashioned
examples: Your grandmother is such a dear woman.
The Hendersons are dear people.

entries.contrast: In British English dear also means expensive; Americans say expensive. Oh dear! is an interjection, and dear is also used to address someone (Thanks, dear).

entries.meaning: Like death, for example in its silence, stillness or paleness. ---
examples: A deathly silence fell over the room.
Her face had a deathly pallor.
The empty streets had a deathly stillness.
entries.contrast: In deathly pale and deathly quiet, deathly is an adverb meaning extremely. Don't confuse it with deadly: a deadly disease is one that kills.

entries.meaning: Made lower in quality, value or moral standards. ---
examples: Critics say reality TV has created a debased culture.
The old coins were made of debased silver.
The word has become debased through overuse.

entries.meaning: Not certain, so people may have different opinions about it. ---
examples: It's debatable whether the new law helped anyone.
That's a debatable point.
Whether it was worth the money is even more debatable.
entries.takes: whether or if clause, usually after It is

entries.meaning: Very weak, especially because of illness. ---
examples: The patient was debilitated after months of chemotherapy.
They cared for debilitated elderly relatives at home.
He seemed more debilitated each time I visited.
entries.form: -ed from debilitate — the person who is weakened
entries.contrast: Debilitated describes the weakened person; debilitating describes the illness or thing that weakens them.

entries.meaning: Making someone very weak or unable to live normally. ---
examples: She suffers from debilitating migraines.
The disease can be debilitating.
Fatigue is one of the most debilitating symptoms.

entries.meaning: Stylish, confident and charming, usually said of a man. ---
examples: He was a debonair man in a white dinner jacket.
The actor looked debonair on the red carpet.
He's even more debonair in person.

entries.meaning: Decadent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Critics attacked the decadent lifestyle of the rich.
The empire grew weak and decadent.
We shared a decadent chocolate cake.
Breakfast in bed felt wonderfully decadent.
It's the most decadent dessert on the menu.

senses.head: Having low moral standards and caring too much about pleasure
examples: Critics attacked the decadent lifestyle of the rich.
The empire grew weak and decadent.

senses.head: Very rich and enjoyable, in a way that feels like a luxury
examples: We shared a decadent chocolate cake.
Breakfast in bed felt wonderfully decadent.
It's the most decadent dessert on the menu.

entries.meaning: Rotten or falling apart because of natural processes. ---
examples: The dentist pulled a decayed tooth.
They found the decayed remains of an old boat.
The wood near the bottom was badly decayed.

entries.meaning: Lying to or tricking people. ---
examples: Her deceitful behavior cost her the job.
He was deceitful with everyone, even his wife.
He was the most deceitful person I've ever worked with.
entries.contrast: Deceitful describes a person who lies and tricks; deceptive describes something that gives a false impression. Russian обманчивый is usually deceptive.

entries.meaning: With power or control spread among many places or people rather than one center. ---
examples: The U.S. has a decentralized school system.
Bitcoin is a decentralized currency.
The company became more decentralized after the merger.

entries.meaning: Giving a false impression, whether on purpose or not. ---
examples: Appearances can be deceptive.
The company was fined for deceptive advertising.
The most deceptive part of the hike is the last mile, which looks flat but isn't.
entries.contrast: Deceptive describes things that give a false impression; deceitful describes people who lie.

entries.meaning: Clear and definite; easy to notice. ---
examples: The home team has a decided advantage.
There was a decided change in his attitude.
She speaks with a decided Southern accent.
entries.contrast: Not решённый: The matter is decided is the verb. Before a noun, decided means clear and definite. The adverb decidedly (decidedly odd) is more common.

entries.meaning: Settling the result of a vote, a game or a choice. ---
examples: The senator cast the deciding vote.
Price was the deciding factor.
They won the deciding game of the series.
entries.contrast: Deciding is the one thing that settles a result (the deciding goal). Decisive can mean that too, but it also describes a person who decides quickly.

entries.meaning: Of a tree or bush, losing its leaves every fall. ---
examples: Oaks and maples are deciduous trees.
In the fall, the deciduous forests turn red and gold.
Most of the shrubs in our yard are deciduous.

entries.meaning: Based on the number ten. ---
examples: Move the decimal point two places to the right.
The metric system is a decimal system.
Round the answer to two decimal places.
entries.contrast: Americans write a decimal point, not a comma: 3.5, said three point five. A decimal is also a noun.

entries.meaning: Decisive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was a decisive victory for the Democrats.
The Battle of Midway was decisive in the Pacific war.
We need a decisive leader.
She's more decisive than her boss.
Be decisive — the offer won't last.

senses.head: Having a strong effect on the result
examples: It was a decisive victory for the Democrats.
The Battle of Midway was decisive in the Pacific war.

senses.head: Able to make decisions quickly and firmly
examples: We need a decisive leader.
She's more decisive than her boss.
Be decisive — the offer won't last.

entries.meaning: Stated officially or publicly. ---
examples: She is a declared candidate for governor.
His declared goal is to cut taxes.
The country has been in a declared state of emergency since June.

entries.meaning: No longer secret, so the public can see it. ---
examples: Historians studied declassified CIA files.
A declassified memo shows the president knew about the plan.
The report is now declassified and available online.

entries.meaning: Decorated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cake was beautifully decorated.
Ours was the most decorated house on the block at Christmas.
He is a highly decorated war veteran.
She's the most decorated gymnast in U.S. history.

senses.head: Made more attractive with added things
examples: The cake was beautifully decorated.
Ours was the most decorated house on the block at Christmas.

senses.head: Having received medals or other honors
examples: He is a highly decorated war veteran.
She's the most decorated gymnast in U.S. history.

entries.meaning: Meant to look attractive rather than to be useful. ---
examples: She bought some decorative pillows for the couch.
The fireplace is only decorative; it doesn't work.
The new design is more decorative than practical.

entries.meaning: Polite and correct in behavior; formal. ---
examples: The guests were quiet and decorous.
They exchanged a decorous kiss on the cheek.
The ceremony was more decorous than the party that followed.

entries.meaning: Smaller in amount, level or number than before. ---
examples: Side effects include decreased appetite.
Exercise is linked to a decreased risk of heart disease.
Workers reported decreased stress after the change.

entries.meaning: Old and in bad condition, or weak because of old age. ---
examples: They bought a decrepit old farmhouse and fixed it up.
The decrepit bus broke down twice on the way.
The building looked even more decrepit in daylight.

entries.meaning: Dedicated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She's a dedicated teacher.
He is dedicated to helping homeless veterans.
No one on the team is more dedicated than Mike.
The hospital has a dedicated children's ward.
We run the website on a dedicated server.

senses.head: Working hard at something because you believe it is important
examples: She's a dedicated teacher.
He is dedicated to helping homeless veterans.
No one on the team is more dedicated than Mike.

senses.head: Made or used for one particular purpose only
examples: The hospital has a dedicated children's ward.
We run the website on a dedicated server.

entries.contrast: After dedicated to, use a noun or -ing, not an infinitive: dedicated to helping, not dedicated to help.

entries.meaning: Able to be subtracted from the income you pay tax on. ---
examples: Donations to the food bank are tax-deductible.
Keep receipts for all deductible business expenses.
Is the cost of my home office deductible?
entries.contrast: In American English a deductible is also a noun: the amount you pay yourself before your insurance pays (a $500 deductible).

entries.meaning: Reaching a conclusion by reasoning from general facts to a particular case. ---
examples: Sherlock Holmes is famous for his deductive reasoning.
The course teaches basic deductive logic.
Math proofs follow a deductive method.

entries.meaning: Deep has 7 distinct senses.
examples: The lake is deeper than it looks.
The kitchen drawers are nice and deep.
Take a deep breath and count to ten.
We had a long, deep conversation about our future.
She has a deep understanding of the law.
That movie was too deep for me.
He has a deep respect for his teachers.
The news caused deep sadness in the town.
The baby finally fell into a deep sleep.
I was in such a deep sleep that I didn't hear the alarm.
He has a deep, calm voice.
We heard the deep sound of a ship's horn.
She wore a deep red dress.
The sky turned a deep blue after sunset.
You're in deep trouble, young man.
The company fell into deep debt.

senses.head: Going a long way down or in from the top, surface or edge
examples: The lake is deeper than it looks.
The kitchen drawers are nice and deep.
Take a deep breath and count to ten.

senses.head: Serious and thoughtful, or showing real understanding
examples: We had a long, deep conversation about our future.
She has a deep understanding of the law.
That movie was too deep for me.

senses.head: Felt very strongly
examples: He has a deep respect for his teachers.
The news caused deep sadness in the town.

senses.head: Of sleep: hard to wake up from
examples: The baby finally fell into a deep sleep.
I was in such a deep sleep that I didn't hear the alarm.

senses.head: Of a voice or sound: low
examples: He has a deep, calm voice.
We heard the deep sound of a ship's horn.

senses.head: Of a color: dark and strong
examples: She wore a deep red dress.
The sky turned a deep blue after sunset.

senses.head: Of trouble, debt or a crisis: very serious
examples: You're in deep trouble, young man.
The company fell into deep debt.

entries.position: both — also after a measurement: six feet deep
entries.contrast: deep is also an adverb of place (dig deep, deep in the woods), but for feelings and degree use deeply: deeply sorry, deeply moved, not deep sorry.

entries.meaning: Cooked by being covered completely in hot oil. ---
examples: The fair sells deep-fried Oreos.
I ordered the deep-fried shrimp.
Everything on this menu is deep-fried.

entries.meaning: Existing for a long time and very hard to change. ---
examples: The town has a deep-rooted distrust of outsiders.
Their love of baseball is deep-rooted.
The problem is more deep-rooted than we thought.

entries.meaning: In or from the deep parts of the ocean. ---
examples: We went deep-sea fishing off the coast of Florida.
Deep-sea divers need special training.
Some deep-sea creatures make their own light.

entries.meaning: Strongly felt or believed and difficult to change. ---
examples: She has a deep-seated fear of failure.
The conflict has deep-seated causes.
His anger seemed deep-seated.

entries.meaning: Of eyes: set far back in the face. ---
examples: He had dark, deep-set eyes.
Her eyes are deep-set, like her mother's.
The actor's deep-set eyes made him look serious.

entries.meaning: Becoming more serious, stronger or greater. ---
examples: The country faces a deepening economic crisis.
There is deepening concern about the water supply.
They watched the deepening shadows in the valley.

entries.meaning: Saying false things that damage someone's reputation. ---
examples: The senator sued the paper over a defamatory article.
The judge ruled that the posts were defamatory.
He was ordered to remove the defamatory statements from his website.

entries.meaning: Defeated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The defeated army retreated to the hills.
The defeated candidate gave a short speech to her supporters.
He walked off the field looking tired and defeated.
She sat at her desk with a defeated look on her face.
I've never felt more defeated in my life.

senses.head: Having lost a battle, game or election
examples: The defeated army retreated to the hills.
The defeated candidate gave a short speech to her supporters.

senses.head: Feeling that you have failed and have no hope left
examples: He walked off the field looking tired and defeated.
She sat at her desk with a defeated look on her face.
I've never felt more defeated in my life.

entries.meaning: Not made correctly or not working correctly. ---
examples: The store replaced the defective phone for free.
The car company recalled thousands of defective airbags.
If the heater is defective, send it back.

entries.meaning: Of a champion: having won the last competition and now trying to win again. ---
examples: The Chiefs are the defending Super Bowl champions.
The defending champion lost in the first round.
She is the defending title holder in the women's race.

entries.meaning: Weak and unable to protect yourself. ---
examples: The wolves attacked a defenseless calf.
Without a lawyer, he felt completely defenseless.
Newborn kittens are among the most defenseless animals.
entries.contrast: American spelling defenseless; British defenceless.

entries.meaning: Defensible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Firing him was a defensible decision.
Her position is legally defensible.
The second plan is more defensible than the first.
The fort was built on a defensible hill.
The soldiers moved to a more defensible position.

senses.head: Able to be supported with good reasons
examples: Firing him was a defensible decision.
Her position is legally defensible.
The second plan is more defensible than the first.

senses.head: Able to be protected from attack
examples: The fort was built on a defensible hill.
The soldiers moved to a more defensible position.

entries.meaning: Defensive has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The country says the missiles are purely defensive.
Take a defensive driving course to lower your insurance.
Why are you getting so defensive? I was only asking.
He gets defensive whenever his mother mentions his job.
She became more defensive with every question.
He plays on the defensive line.
It was the best defensive game of the season.

senses.head: Used or done to protect against attack
examples: The country says the missiles are purely defensive.
Take a defensive driving course to lower your insurance.

senses.head: Reacting as if you are being criticized or attacked
examples: Why are you getting so defensive? I was only asking.
He gets defensive whenever his mother mentions his job.
She became more defensive with every question.

senses.head: In sports: trying to stop the other team from scoring
examples: He plays on the defensive line.
It was the best defensive game of the season.

entries.meaning: Showing polite respect, often by agreeing with or obeying someone. ---
examples: The staff were very deferential to the new owner.
He spoke in a quiet, deferential voice.
Younger doctors were more deferential back then.

entries.meaning: Openly refusing to obey or to accept something. ---
examples: The teenager gave his father a defiant look.
Even after losing, the fans remained defiant.
The protesters grew more defiant as the police moved in.

entries.meaning: Not having enough of something that is needed. ---
examples: Many people are deficient in vitamin D in the winter.
The soil here is deficient in iron.
The report called the safety checks seriously deficient.
entries.contrast: Not Russian дефицитный (hard to find): deficient means lacking something needed. A scarce product is hard to find or in short supply.

entries.meaning: Defined has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's been working out and his arms are more defined now.
The shadows in the photo are sharply defined.
Everyone on the team has a clearly defined role.

The villain's schemes grow more devilish with every episode.

entries.meaning: Devout has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Sincere and deeply committed to a cause, team or belief

entries.meaning: Skillful with the hands, or clever in handling a situation. ---

The nurse works with diabetic children.

senses.head: Caused by diabetes or made for people who have it

The store has a shelf of diabetic snacks.

entries.meaning: Extremely evil, cruel or cunning. ---

Each trap in the game is more diabolical than the last.

entries.meaning: Used to find out what illness or problem someone or something has. ---

The mechanic ran a diagnostic check on the engine.
A high fever alone isn't diagnostic of the flu.

His tone became more didactic as the lecture went on.

The museum's exhibits are mostly didactic.

entries.meaning: Relating to the food a person eats. ---

entries.meaning: Differential has 2 distinct senses.

The airline uses differential pricing for weekends.

senses.head: In math, relating to rates of change

The course covers differential calculus.

entries.contrast: A differential is also a noun: a pay differential, or the gear box between a car's wheels.

entries.meaning: Shy and lacking confidence. ---

entries.contrast: Do not confuse with different: diffident means shy and unsure of yourself.

senses.head: Spread out over a wide area, not concentrated in one place
examples: The lamp gives off soft, diffuse light.
Power in the company is diffuse, with no clear leader.

senses.head: Of writing or speech, long and unfocused
examples: The essay was long and diffuse.
His argument became more diffuse as he went on.

entries.meaning: Digestible has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Of food, easy for the body to digest

The newspaper has more digital subscribers than print ones.

senses.head: Showing information as numbers rather than with hands or a pointer
examples: I bought a cheap digital watch.

entries.meaning: Calm, serious and deserving respect. ---

entries.meaning: Of a building or vehicle, old and falling apart from neglect. ---

entries.meaning: Working hard and carefully. ---

senses.head: Of an idea or plan, made weaker or less effective

The message gets more diluted each time it's passed on.

It's a disgraceful waste of taxpayers' money.
