entries.meaning: Annoyed and unhappy, especially because you feel treated unfairly. ---
examples: A disgruntled former employee hacked the system.
Customers are disgruntled about the price increase.
Fans grew more disgruntled as the losses piled up.

entries.meaning: Disguised has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The thief entered the building disguised as a delivery man.
Police used a disguised van to watch the house.
It was a thinly disguised attack on his rival.
She listened with barely disguised impatience.

senses.head: Changed in appearance so as not to be recognized
examples: The thief entered the building disguised as a delivery man.
Police used a disguised van to watch the house.

senses.head: Of a feeling or intention, hidden but still noticeable
examples: It was a thinly disguised attack on his rival.
She listened with barely disguised impatience.

entries.comparison: not gradable — sense 2 often with thinly or barely
entries.takes: as + noun, for what someone or something is made to look like

entries.meaning: Having lost hope or enthusiasm. ---
examples: Don't be disheartened by one bad review.
The disheartened players walked off the field in silence.
I was more disheartened by his silence than by his words.
entries.form: -ed — how you feel; what causes it is disheartening

entries.meaning: Making you lose hope or enthusiasm. ---
examples: It's disheartening to see so much trash on the beach.
We got some disheartening news from the doctor.
The most disheartening part was how little anyone cared.
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling; the person feels disheartened

entries.meaning: Of a person, hair or clothes, messy and untidy. ---
examples: He showed up late, tired and disheveled.
Her hair was disheveled from the wind.
After the red-eye flight, he looked even more disheveled than usual.
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l: disheveled. British English writes dishevelled.

entries.meaning: Not honest; lying, cheating or stealing. ---
examples: It would be dishonest to pretend I like it.
He was fired for dishonest behavior.
Politicians aren't any more dishonest than the rest of us.
entries.form: dis- + honest — the h is silent

entries.meaning: Shameful and not deserving respect. ---
examples: He received a dishonorable discharge from the Army.
Lying to your own team is dishonorable.
There's nothing more dishonorable than betraying a friend.
entries.form: dis- + honorable — American spelling, no u

entries.meaning: Disappointed because something is not as good as you believed. ---
examples: Many young people are disillusioned with politics.
She left teaching tired and disillusioned.
The more disillusioned voters simply stayed home.

entries.meaning: Not wanting to do something. ---
examples: I was disinclined to believe him.
She seemed disinclined to help.
After the meeting, he was even more disinclined to sign.

entries.meaning: Not sincere; pretending to be honest or innocent. ---
examples: It's disingenuous to say you didn't know.
Her apology sounded disingenuous.
That's the most disingenuous excuse I've heard.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with ingenious (clever): disingenuous means pretending to be honest or to know less than you do.

entries.meaning: Not well connected, so hard to follow. ---
examples: The movie felt disjointed and hard to follow.
He gave a disjointed account of the accident.
The second half of the book is more disjointed than the first.

entries.meaning: Dislocated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's out for a month with a dislocated shoulder.
The doctor popped my dislocated finger back into place.
The war left millions of dislocated families.
Workers felt dislocated after the factory moved overseas.

senses.head: Of a bone or joint, pushed out of its normal position
examples: He's out for a month with a dislocated shoulder.
The doctor popped my dislocated finger back into place.

senses.head: Forced away from home or a familiar place, and feeling lost
examples: The war left millions of dislocated families.
Workers felt dislocated after the factory moved overseas.

entries.meaning: Not loyal; not supporting your friends, family, country or group. ---
examples: He was accused of being disloyal to the party.
It felt disloyal to criticize my own family.
The president fired advisers he saw as disloyal.

entries.meaning: Dismal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was a cold, dismal day in February.
The future looked dismal.
The team had a dismal season.
Sales were even more dismal than expected.
His test scores were dismal.

senses.head: Gloomy and depressing
examples: It was a cold, dismal day in February.
The future looked dismal.

senses.head: Very bad or unsuccessful
examples: The team had a dismal season.
Sales were even more dismal than expected.
His test scores were dismal.

entries.meaning: Shocked, worried and disappointed. ---
examples: We were dismayed to learn the park had closed.
Fans were dismayed by the trade.
No one was more dismayed than the coach.
entries.takes: at or by + noun; to-infinitive; that-clause

entries.meaning: Showing that you think something is not worth considering. ---
examples: He was dismissive of my concerns.
She waved her hand in a dismissive gesture.
The doctor was even more dismissive the second time.

entries.meaning: Refusing to do what you are told. ---
examples: The disobedient dog kept jumping on guests.
The kids were tired and disobedient.
He's more disobedient with his mom than with his dad.

entries.meaning: Disorderly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The papers were piled in a disorderly heap.
His desk is always disorderly.
He was arrested for disorderly conduct.
The crowd grew more disorderly as the night went on.

senses.head: Untidy and messy
examples: The papers were piled in a disorderly heap.
His desk is always disorderly.

senses.head: Noisy, rowdy and breaking public order
examples: He was arrested for disorderly conduct.
The crowd grew more disorderly as the night went on.

entries.contrast: It ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb. Disorderly conduct is a legal charge in the US, like Russian мелкое хулиганство.

entries.meaning: Badly planned, or not good at planning and keeping things in order. ---
examples: I'm so disorganized — I can never find my keys.
The event was chaotic and disorganized.
Their campaign was more disorganized than anyone expected.

entries.meaning: Confused about where you are, what time it is or what is happening. ---
examples: She woke up disoriented in a hospital bed.
The fog left the hikers disoriented.
He seemed more disoriented after the second fall.
entries.form: -ed — how you feel; what causes it is disorienting
entries.contrast: American English says disoriented; British English also uses disorientated.

entries.meaning: Making you confused about where you are or what is happening. ---
examples: Flying across several time zones can be disorienting.
The hospital's maze of hallways was disorienting.
The most disorienting part was losing track of the days.
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling; the person feels disoriented

entries.meaning: Criticizing someone or something in a way that shows no respect. ---
examples: He made disparaging remarks about her weight.
The review was openly disparaging of the director.
Her comments grew more disparaging over time.

entries.meaning: So different from each other that they are hard to compare or combine. ---
examples: The band mixes disparate styles like jazz and punk.
The two groups have very disparate goals.
It's hard to unite such disparate communities.
entries.contrast: Don't confuse with desperate (DES-pur-uht): disparate means very different from each other.

entries.meaning: Not influenced by emotion; calm and fair. ---
examples: We need a dispassionate look at the facts.
Judges must remain dispassionate.
A more dispassionate observer might see it differently.

entries.meaning: Not necessary; easy to do without or replace. ---
examples: In a crisis, some staff are seen as dispensable.
Nobody on this team is dispensable.
Workers felt more dispensable after the robots arrived.

entries.meaning: Having lost hope and energy. ---
examples: The volunteers went home tired and dispirited.
A dispirited crowd filed out before the last inning.
She sounded more dispirited than angry on the phone.
entries.contrast: Dispirited is how the people feel; dispiriting is what causes the feeling: a dispiriting loss left the team dispirited.

entries.meaning: Making you lose hope and energy. ---
examples: It was a dispiriting end to a good season.
The turnout was dispiriting, even to the organizers.
Nothing is more dispiriting than a job search that goes nowhere.
entries.contrast: Use dispiriting for the thing and dispirited for the person: a dispiriting report, a dispirited staff.

entries.meaning: Annoyed or not satisfied, in a controlled, formal way. ---
examples: The principal was clearly displeased with our excuse.
Shareholders are displeased at the pace of the layoffs.
She looked displeased but said nothing.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: she was displeased
entries.takes: with or at + noun; by + what caused it
entries.contrast: A formal, slightly cool word — much milder than angry. Bosses and judges are displeased; friends are just annoyed.

entries.meaning: Causing annoyance or dissatisfaction. ---
examples: The design was displeasing to almost everyone on the board.
He has a displeasing habit of talking over people.
Nothing about the room was displeasing, but nothing charmed us either.

entries.meaning: Disposable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The party ran on disposable plates and cups.
She packed disposable razors for the trip.
Disposable diapers fill the trash fast.
Families here have less disposable income than they did in 2019.
Teenagers with disposable cash drive the whole market.

senses.head: Made to be thrown away after one use
examples: The party ran on disposable plates and cups.
She packed disposable razors for the trip.
Disposable diapers fill the trash fast.

senses.head: Of money: left over after taxes and bills, free to spend
examples: Families here have less disposable income than they did in 2019.
Teenagers with disposable cash drive the whole market.

entries.contrast: Also a noun in the plural: the hospital buys disposables by the case.

entries.meaning: Disposed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The judge was not disposed to grant another delay.
I'd be more disposed to help if he'd asked politely.
The committee seems well disposed toward our proposal.
He was kindly disposed to every stray that showed up.

senses.head: Willing or inclined to do something
examples: The judge was not disposed to grant another delay.
I'd be more disposed to help if he'd asked politely.

senses.head: Feeling friendly or unfriendly toward someone or something
examples: The committee seems well disposed toward our proposal.
He was kindly disposed to every stray that showed up.

entries.position: predicative only — I'm not disposed to argue
entries.takes: to-infinitive — willing; toward or to + person, after well or kindly — friendly
entries.contrast: Formal. In the 'friendly' sense it needs well, kindly or ill in front: well disposed toward the plan. Do not confuse it with disposable (thrown away after use).

entries.meaning: Too large or too small compared with something else. ---
examples: The fine seems disproportionate to the offense.
A disproportionate share of the cuts fell on rural schools.
Their spending on travel is disproportionate, given the budget.

entries.meaning: Not agreed on — argued over by two or more sides. ---
examples: Troops are massed along the disputed border.
The bill for the repairs is still disputed.
He won a disputed election by fewer than a thousand votes.

entries.meaning: Making someone unfit or ineligible for a job, a prize or a competition. ---
examples: A felony conviction is a disqualifying factor for this license.
The doctor found no disqualifying condition.
For most voters it wasn't a disqualifying mistake.

entries.meaning: Making you feel worried or uneasy. ---
examples: The report makes disquieting reading.
There's something disquieting about how quiet the street is.
The most disquieting part is that nobody noticed for a month.

entries.meaning: Having a bad reputation; not to be trusted or respected. ---
examples: He borrowed money from a disreputable lender.
The bar had the most disreputable crowd in town.
Her landlord is disreputable but not quite a criminal.

entries.meaning: Showing no respect for someone or something. ---
examples: Don't be disrespectful to your grandmother.
Leaving in the middle of her speech was disrespectful.
That was the most disrespectful thing he's ever said to a teacher.
entries.takes: to or toward + person; of + thing

entries.meaning: Disruptive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Two disruptive students were sent to the office.
The construction has been disruptive to the whole block.
Late-night noise is more disruptive than she realizes.
Streaming was the most disruptive thing to hit the music business.
They pitch every app as disruptive innovation.

senses.head: Interrupting something and stopping it from going normally
examples: Two disruptive students were sent to the office.
The construction has been disruptive to the whole block.
Late-night noise is more disruptive than she realizes.

senses.head: Of a technology or business: changing an industry completely
examples: Streaming was the most disruptive thing to hit the music business.
They pitch every app as disruptive innovation.

entries.русский: мешающий, нарушающий порядок; радикально меняющий рынок

entries.meaning: Not happy with something because it is not good enough. ---
examples: Customers are dissatisfied with the new billing system.
A dissatisfied employee will find another job by spring.
The longer she waited, the more dissatisfied she got.
entries.contrast: Dissatisfied means unhappy with what you got; unsatisfied means you did not get enough (an unsatisfied appetite, an unsatisfied claim).

entries.meaning: Disagreeing with the official or majority view. ---
examples: Two justices filed a dissenting opinion.
There were a few dissenting voices at the town meeting.
The board approved it with one dissenting vote.
entries.contrast: In court reporting, a dissenting opinion is the written opinion of a judge who voted the other way.

entries.meaning: Openly opposing an official policy, especially a government's. ---
examples: Dissident writers were published abroad.
The party expelled its dissident wing.
She spent six years in a camp for dissident activity.
entries.contrast: Far more common as a noun: The dissidents were released in 1989.

entries.meaning: Not alike. ---
examples: Her style is not dissimilar to her mother's.
The two engines are more dissimilar than they look.
They came from wildly dissimilar backgrounds.
entries.contrast: Often in the understatement not dissimilar to, which means 'fairly similar to'.

entries.meaning: Able to be dissolved in a liquid, or to break down inside the body. ---
examples: The surgeon used dissolvable stitches.
These are dissolvable tablets — drop one in water.
The packaging is dissolvable in hot water.
entries.contrast: Chemists and food labels prefer soluble; dissolvable is the everyday word, and the usual one for stitches and tablets.

entries.meaning: Distant has 4 distinct senses.
examples: We could see the lights of a distant town.
The telescope picks up the most distant galaxies.
Retirement still feels distant.
In the not too distant future, all of this will be automated.
He's a distant cousin on my father's side.
They're distant relatives who meet once a decade.
She's been distant with me since the argument.
He had a distant look, as if he hadn't heard the question.

senses.head: Far away in space
examples: We could see the lights of a distant town.
The telescope picks up the most distant galaxies.

senses.head: Far away in time, in the past or the future
examples: Retirement still feels distant.
In the not too distant future, all of this will be automated.

senses.head: Related only slightly, in a family
examples: He's a distant cousin on my father's side.
They're distant relatives who meet once a decade.

senses.head: Cold and unfriendly, or lost in thought
examples: She's been distant with me since the argument.
He had a distant look, as if he hadn't heard the question.

entries.meaning: Unpleasant or offensive, especially to your sense of what is decent. ---
examples: The ad was distasteful and got pulled in a day.
Firing people by email is distasteful to most managers.
He found the whole business more distasteful the longer it went on.
entries.contrast: It is about morals and manners, not food: a joke can be distasteful, but soup that tastes bad is just awful. Tasteless is the closer opposite of tasteful.

entries.meaning: Distinct has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Spanish and Portuguese are distinct languages.
The job has two distinct parts.
Keep your work email distinct from your personal one.
There was a distinct smell of gas in the hall.
I got the distinct impression she wanted us to leave.

senses.head: Clearly separate and different from something else
examples: Spanish and Portuguese are distinct languages.
The job has two distinct parts.
Keep your work email distinct from your personal one.

senses.head: Easily seen, heard or smelled; unmistakable
examples: There was a distinct smell of gas in the hall.
I got the distinct impression she wanted us to leave.

entries.contrast: Distinct means separate or clear; distinctive means recognizable as belonging to one person or thing. Her voice is distinct = you hear it clearly; her voice is distinctive = you know it's hers.

entries.meaning: Easy to recognize because it belongs to one person or thing and nothing else. ---
examples: The bird has a distinctive white stripe on its head.
Her handwriting is distinctive — I'd know it anywhere.
Of all their albums, the first has the most distinctive sound.
entries.contrast: Distinctive marks a thing out as its own; distinguished means respected and successful. A distinctive hat, a distinguished professor.

entries.meaning: Able to be told apart from something else, or made out clearly. ---
examples: The copy is barely distinguishable from the original.
In the fog, the shore was hardly distinguishable.
The twins were more distinguishable once one cut his hair.

entries.meaning: Distinguished has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She had a distinguished career in public health.
Our guest tonight is the most distinguished alumna of the school.
He looks distinguished in that gray suit.
A distinguished older gentleman held the door for us.

senses.head: Respected and successful after a long career
examples: She had a distinguished career in public health.
Our guest tonight is the most distinguished alumna of the school.

senses.head: Looking dignified and impressive, often because of gray hair
examples: He looks distinguished in that gray suit.
A distinguished older gentleman held the door for us.

entries.meaning: Distorted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The guitar had a fuzzy, distorted sound.
Our faces looked distorted in the funhouse mirror.
The quote appeared in a badly distorted form online.
He has a distorted picture of what the job involves.

senses.head: Pulled or twisted out of its normal shape or sound
examples: The guitar had a fuzzy, distorted sound.
Our faces looked distorted in the funhouse mirror.

senses.head: Changed so that it gives a false idea of the truth
examples: The quote appeared in a badly distorted form online.
He has a distorted picture of what the job involves.

entries.meaning: Unable to pay attention because something has pulled your mind away. ---
examples: Sorry, I'm distracted — my phone won't stop buzzing.
Distracted driving causes thousands of crashes a year.
She seemed more distracted than usual at dinner.
entries.contrast: Distracted is the person; distracting is the thing: the noise was distracting, and I got distracted.

entries.meaning: So upset that you cannot think or act normally. ---
examples: The distraught mother begged for help finding her son.
He was distraught over the loss of the dog.
She was too distraught to finish the sentence.
entries.contrast: Much stronger than upset — it is the word for a parent whose child is missing.

entries.meaning: Distressed has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Neighbors were distressed by the news.
A distressed passenger was taken off the plane.
She wore distressed jeans and a white tee.
The table has a distressed finish.
The fund buys distressed properties cheap.
Several distressed banks were sold off that year.

senses.head: Very upset or worried
examples: Neighbors were distressed by the news.
A distressed passenger was taken off the plane.

senses.head: Of jeans, leather or furniture: made to look worn and old on purpose
examples: She wore distressed jeans and a white tee.
The table has a distressed finish.

senses.head: In serious financial trouble
examples: The fund buys distressed properties cheap.
Several distressed banks were sold off that year.

entries.meaning: Making you feel upset or worried. ---
examples: The video is distressing to watch.
It's distressing how little anyone knew.
The most distressing part was the silence from the hospital.
entries.contrast: The thing is distressing; the person is distressed.

entries.meaning: Distributed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The weight is evenly distributed across the four legs.
Rainfall is unevenly distributed through the year.
They run a distributed database across three data centers.
We're a fully distributed company with nobody in an office.

senses.head: Spread out over an area or among people rather than gathered in one place
examples: The weight is evenly distributed across the four legs.
Rainfall is unevenly distributed through the year.

senses.head: Of a computer system or a team: split across many machines or locations
examples: They run a distributed database across three data centers.
We're a fully distributed company with nobody in an office.

entries.comparison: not gradable — evenly distributed, widely distributed

entries.meaning: Not willing to trust someone or something. ---
examples: Voters are distrustful of both parties.
Years in the business left him distrustful.
She grew more distrustful with every broken promise.

entries.meaning: Disturbed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Parents were disturbed by what they saw in the video.
I'm deeply disturbed about the direction this is going.
The letters came from a disturbed young man.
He works with emotionally disturbed teenagers.

senses.head: Worried or upset by something
examples: Parents were disturbed by what they saw in the video.
I'm deeply disturbed about the direction this is going.

senses.head: Having serious mental or emotional problems
examples: The letters came from a disturbed young man.
He works with emotionally disturbed teenagers.

entries.contrast: Calling a person disturbed with no adverb suggests mental illness, so say disturbed by the news when you only mean worried.

entries.meaning: Making you feel worried, shocked or upset. ---
examples: The footage is disturbing, so we won't show all of it.
There's a disturbing pattern in these numbers.
The most disturbing thing is how normal he seemed.
entries.contrast: The report is disturbing; the reader is disturbed.

entries.meaning: No longer used, and left empty or idle. ---
examples: Kids broke into the disused factory.
The trail follows a disused rail line.
They store hay in the disused barn.
entries.contrast: The s is /z/: dis-YOOZD. Unused means never used at all; disused means used once but not anymore.

entries.meaning: Going in different directions, or differing from one another. ---
examples: The two reports reach wildly divergent conclusions.
Their paths grew more divergent after college.
His account is divergent from everything the witnesses said.

entries.meaning: Diverse has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The park protects a diverse set of habitats.
Her interests are unusually diverse.
It's the most diverse class the school has ever had.
The neighborhood is far more diverse than it was in 1990.

senses.head: Made up of many different kinds
examples: The park protects a diverse set of habitats.
Her interests are unusually diverse.

senses.head: Including people of many races, backgrounds and cultures
examples: It's the most diverse class the school has ever had.
The neighborhood is far more diverse than it was in 1990.

entries.meaning: Spread across several different kinds of business, product or investment. ---
examples: Keep a diversified portfolio and don't panic.
The company is more diversified than its competitors.
A diversified farm survives a bad year for one crop.

entries.meaning: Meant to draw attention away from something more important. ---
examples: The fire was a diversionary tactic while they emptied the safe.
Critics called the hearing a diversionary move.
Troops staged a diversionary attack on the south road.

entries.meaning: Divine has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They believed the king ruled by divine right.
The painting shows divine light falling on the shepherds.
That chocolate cake was divine.
Her new apartment is the most divine place you've ever seen.

senses.head: Coming from God or belonging to a god
examples: They believed the king ruled by divine right.
The painting shows divine light falling on the shepherds.

senses.head: Wonderful — an informal, old-fashioned word of praise
examples: That chocolate cake was divine.
Her new apartment is the most divine place you've ever seen.

entries.contrast: Sense 1 does not grade — nothing is more divine than God. Only the informal 'wonderful' sense takes more and most, and it sounds dated or theatrical.

entries.meaning: Able to be divided, especially with nothing left over. ---
examples: Nine is divisible by three.
The land is divisible into four equal lots.
Any even number is divisible by two.

entries.meaning: Belonging to one division of a company, an army or a sports league. ---
examples: The divisional manager flew in for the meeting.
They clinched the divisional title in September.
Each divisional office sets its own hours.

entries.meaning: Causing disagreement and splitting people into opposing groups. ---
examples: Immigration is the most divisive issue on the ballot.
His speech was divisive, even inside his own party.
Nothing is more divisive at a family dinner than politics.
entries.contrast: Stress the second syllable and say it with the vowel of eye: dih-VY-siv.

entries.meaning: Divorced has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My parents have been divorced since I was six.
She's a divorced mother of three.
He got divorced last spring.
The plan is divorced from reality.
Their pay is entirely divorced from performance.

senses.head: No longer married, because the marriage was legally ended
examples: My parents have been divorced since I was six.
She's a divorced mother of three.
He got divorced last spring.

senses.head: Completely separated from something, with no connection left
examples: The plan is divorced from reality.
Their pay is entirely divorced from performance.

entries.meaning: Dizzy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I stood up too fast and felt dizzy.
The medicine makes her dizzier than the illness did.
We climbed to a dizzy height above the canyon.
Prices rose at a dizzy pace all summer.

senses.head: Feeling as if everything is spinning and you might fall
examples: I stood up too fast and felt dizzy.
The medicine makes her dizzier than the illness did.

senses.head: Making you feel that way — of heights, speed or a steep rise
examples: We climbed to a dizzy height above the canyon.
Prices rose at a dizzy pace all summer.

entries.meaning: Made or done by ordinary people at home instead of by professionals. ---
examples: The store has a whole do-it-yourself aisle.
She followed a do-it-yourself guide to tiling the bathroom.
It's a do-it-yourself kit, so bring a screwdriver.
entries.form: compound — the whole phrase do it yourself used as one adjective
entries.contrast: Usually shortened to DIY. It is also a noun: He's into do-it-yourself.

entries.meaning: Lazy or useless because it takes no action — usually said in anger about politicians. ---
examples: He campaigned against a do-nothing Congress.
The council has a do-nothing reputation.
They're tired of do-nothing leadership at city hall.
entries.form: compound — the phrase do nothing used as one adjective

entries.meaning: Where you must succeed now or lose everything. ---
examples: Saturday is a do-or-die game for the Jets.
The startup is in a do-or-die month.
She went in with a do-or-die attitude.
entries.form: compound — the phrase do or die used as one adjective

entries.meaning: Possible to do, especially in the time or with the money you have. ---
examples: Two weeks is tight, but it's doable.
Break it into doable steps.
Cutting ten percent is more doable than cutting thirty.
entries.contrast: Informal but common at work. In writing, feasible is the formal choice.

entries.meaning: Quiet and easy to control or lead. ---
examples: The mare is docile enough for a beginner.
He expected a docile audience and got an angry one.
The older dog is much more docile than the puppy.
entries.contrast: Americans say DAH-suhl; the British DOH-syl is not used here.

entries.meaning: Connected with the highest university degree, the doctorate. ---
examples: She's writing her doctoral dissertation on wetlands.
He teaches in the doctoral program in economics.
Doctoral students get a small stipend.
entries.contrast: In the United States a doctoral program leads to a PhD, not to a medical degree.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the official beliefs of a church, a party or a school of thought. ---
examples: The split was doctrinal, not personal.
They argued for years over a small doctrinal point.
The seminary teaches the church's doctrinal history.

entries.meaning: Of a book or paper: worn, with the corners of the pages folded over. ---
examples: He carries a dog-eared paperback in his coat pocket.
The recipe card is stained and dog-eared.
She handed me a dog-eared copy of the map.

entries.meaning: Refusing to give up, however long it takes. ---
examples: Her dogged reporting finally broke the story.
It took dogged persistence to get the permit.
He was the most dogged investigator on the force.
entries.contrast: The adjective has two syllables, DAW-gid. The past tense of the verb dog is one syllable: Reporters dogged him for weeks /dɔːɡd/.

entries.meaning: Insisting that your beliefs are right and refusing to consider anything else. ---
examples: He's dogmatic about how coffee should be made.
The book takes a dogmatic line on diet.
She got more dogmatic as the argument went on.

entries.meaning: Dressed up in fancy clothes and makeup for an occasion. ---
examples: She got all dolled up for the reunion.
Why are you so dolled up on a Tuesday?
The girls came downstairs dolled up and ready for pictures.
entries.position: predicative only — usually all dolled up
entries.form: from the phrasal verb doll up
entries.contrast: Informal and a little old-fashioned, and usually said about women. For a man you would say all dressed up.

entries.meaning: Having the round, curved shape of a dome, or covered by one. ---
examples: The domed roof lets light into the hall.
They play in a domed stadium, so rain never matters.
The lid is slightly domed so the steam runs off.

entries.meaning: Domestic has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Domestic flights leave from Terminal B.
Most of the company's sales are domestic.
The police were called to a domestic dispute.
She handles most of the domestic chores.
The shelter takes domestic animals only.
Cats were domestic long before they were pets.

senses.head: Inside one country, not foreign
examples: Domestic flights leave from Terminal B.
Most of the company's sales are domestic.

senses.head: Having to do with the home and family
examples: The police were called to a domestic dispute.
She handles most of the domestic chores.

senses.head: Of an animal: kept by people, not wild
examples: The shelter takes domestic animals only.
Cats were domestic long before they were pets.

entries.meaning: Domesticated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Horses were domesticated thousands of years ago.
A domesticated fox still isn't a dog.
Since the baby, he's completely domesticated.
My brother is more domesticated than I'll ever be.

senses.head: Of an animal or plant: bred and kept by people instead of living wild
examples: Horses were domesticated thousands of years ago.
A domesticated fox still isn't a dog.

senses.head: Of a person: happy doing housework and staying home — usually a joke
examples: Since the baby, he's completely domesticated.
My brother is more domesticated than I'll ever be.

entries.meaning: Dominant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The company is dominant in three states.
Oak is the dominant tree in these woods.
She was the most dominant player in the league that year.
Brown eyes come from a dominant gene.
The trait is dominant, so half the litter will show it.

senses.head: Most powerful, most important or most noticeable
examples: The company is dominant in three states.
Oak is the dominant tree in these woods.
She was the most dominant player in the league that year.

senses.head: Of a gene: showing its effect even when only one parent passes it on
examples: Brown eyes come from a dominant gene.
The trait is dominant, so half the litter will show it.

entries.meaning: Dominating has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was a dominating performance from the freshman.
The defense was dominating in the second half.
The cathedral is the dominating feature of the skyline.
He has a dominating presence in any room.

senses.head: Controlling a game, a market or a scene completely
examples: It was a dominating performance from the freshman.
The defense was dominating in the second half.

senses.head: Standing over everything else and drawing all the attention
examples: The cathedral is the dominating feature of the skyline.
He has a dominating presence in any room.

entries.contrast: Dominating describes a performance or a presence; domineering is always an insult about a person who bosses others around.

entries.meaning: Trying to control other people and give them orders. ---
examples: She grew up with a domineering stepfather.
He gets domineering the moment he's put in charge.
The coach is the most domineering man I've ever worked for.

entries.meaning: From or connected with the Dominican Republic. ---
examples: We ate at a Dominican restaurant in Washington Heights.
Dominican players fill half the roster.
Her mother is Dominican and her father is Cuban.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: She's a Dominican. Capital D always. The same word names the Dominican order of friars.

entries.meaning: Done has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The laundry is done.
Give me ten minutes and I'll be done.
Once the paperwork is done, you get the keys.
Check whether the chicken is done in the middle.
I like my burger more done than that.
The merger is a done deal.
Don't treat the promotion as done until you sign something.

senses.head: Finished; completed
examples: The laundry is done.
Give me ten minutes and I'll be done.
Once the paperwork is done, you get the keys.

senses.head: Of food: cooked enough
examples: Check whether the chicken is done in the middle.
I like my burger more done than that.

senses.head: Settled and no longer open to change — in a done deal
examples: The merger is a done deal.
Don't treat the promotion as done until you sign something.

entries.position: predicative only — before a noun only in fixed phrases: a done deal
entries.comparison: not gradable — but food can be more done, well done
entries.contrast: Americans say I'm done for 'I have finished'. Well done on a steak means cooked through; said to a person it is praise.

entries.meaning: Certain to fail, be ruined or die. ---
examples: If the power goes out now, we're done for.
Without that contract the shop is done for.
One more penalty and they're done for.
entries.contrast: Informal and never before a noun. It can be a joke about losing a game or serious about dying.

entries.meaning: Finished using or dealing with something, or refusing to deal with it any longer. ---
examples: Are you done with the scissors?
I'm done with apologizing for him.
After that phone call she was done with the whole family.
entries.русский: покончивший (с чем-либо), больше не имеющий дела
entries.position: predicative only — I'm done with it
entries.takes: with + noun or -ing — the with is part of the phrase
entries.contrast: Done with a thing can mean you have simply finished using it; done with a person means the relationship is over.

entries.meaning: Certain to fail, suffer or be destroyed. ---
examples: The plan was doomed from the start.
He plays a doomed soldier in the film.
Without water the crop is doomed to fail.

entries.meaning: Going from one house to the next, or delivered from the sender's door to the receiver's. ---
examples: He worked as a door-to-door salesman for two summers.
The campaign relies on door-to-door canvassing.
We pay extra for door-to-door delivery.
entries.contrast: As an adverb it usually drops the hyphens: They went door to door collecting signatures.

entries.meaning: Dopey has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The pills leave me dopey all morning.
He was still dopey from the anesthesia.
He has a dopey grin in every photo.
That's the dopiest excuse I've heard all week.

senses.head: Sleepy and slow-thinking, usually from medicine or lack of sleep
examples: The pills leave me dopey all morning.
He was still dopey from the anesthesia.

senses.head: Silly or a little stupid
examples: He has a dopey grin in every photo.
That's the dopiest excuse I've heard all week.

entries.contrast: Informal. Note the spelling with -e-: dopey, but dopier and dopiest.

entries.meaning: Dormant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The volcano has been dormant for two centuries.
The virus can stay dormant in the body for years.
A dormant account gets closed after eighteen months.
Prune the roses while they're dormant.
The seeds lie dormant until the first warm rain.

senses.head: Not active now, but able to become active again
examples: The volcano has been dormant for two centuries.
The virus can stay dormant in the body for years.
A dormant account gets closed after eighteen months.

senses.head: Of a plant or seed: alive but not growing, usually over winter
examples: Prune the roses while they're dormant.
The seeds lie dormant until the first warm rain.

entries.meaning: Having to do with internet companies, especially those of the late 1990s boom. ---
examples: He made and lost a fortune in the dot-com boom.
Her parents met at a dot-com startup in 1999.
The dot-com crash emptied half the office park.
entries.form: compound — from the web address ending .com
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a failed dot-com. It usually points back to the internet boom of the late 1990s.

entries.meaning: Loving someone so much that you spoil them and see no fault. ---
examples: Her doting grandfather bought her a pony.
He's a doting father of three.
She married the most doting man in the county.
entries.contrast: The verb needs on: She dotes on her nephews. The adjective goes straight before a noun: a doting aunt.

entries.meaning: Dotted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Sign on the dotted line.
She wore a dotted blue dress.
The hillside is dotted with white farmhouses.
The lawn was dotted with dandelions by May.

senses.head: Made of or marked with dots
examples: Sign on the dotted line.
She wore a dotted blue dress.

senses.head: Covered with small things spread here and there
examples: The hillside is dotted with white farmhouses.
The lawn was dotted with dandelions by May.

entries.meaning: Double has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He earns double what I do.
Order a double shot if you're driving tonight.
The barn has double doors at both ends.
Her name has a double l in it.
We booked a double room with a view.
The guest bed is a double, not a queen.

senses.head: Twice as much, as many or as big
examples: He earns double what I do.
Order a double shot if you're driving tonight.

senses.head: Made of two similar parts, or having two of something
examples: The barn has double doors at both ends.
Her name has a double l in it.

senses.head: Meant for two people
examples: We booked a double room with a view.
The guest bed is a double, not a queen.

entries.contrast: Double is also a verb (Prices doubled) and a noun (a double at the bar). Before a noun it needs no of: double the price, not double of the price.

entries.meaning: Double-barreled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He keeps a double-barreled shotgun in the truck.
The museum has a double-barreled cannon out front.
That's a double-barreled question — answer one part at a time.
The storm was a double-barreled hit of wind and flooding.

senses.head: Of a gun: having two barrels
examples: He keeps a double-barreled shotgun in the truck.
The museum has a double-barreled cannon out front.

senses.head: Doing two things at once, or having two parts
examples: That's a double-barreled question — answer one part at a time.
The storm was a double-barreled hit of wind and flooding.

entries.contrast: American spelling has one l: double-barreled. The British write double-barrelled.

entries.meaning: Of a coat or jacket: with two rows of buttons and fronts that overlap. ---
examples: He wore a navy double-breasted blazer.
Double-breasted suits came back in style.
She found a double-breasted wool coat at the thrift store.

entries.meaning: Cheating people by secretly working for both sides. ---
examples: They found out about his double-dealing partner too late.
It was a double-dealing scheme from day one.
She has no patience for double-dealing politicians.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: He was fired for double-dealing.

entries.meaning: Double-edged has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The knife has a double-edged blade.
He collects double-edged razors.
Fame is a double-edged sword.
The tax break is a double-edged gift for small towns.

senses.head: Of a blade: sharp on both sides
examples: The knife has a double-edged blade.
He collects double-edged razors.

senses.head: Having a good effect and a bad one at the same time
body: (имеющий две стороны, как палка о двух концах)
examples: Fame is a double-edged sword.
The tax break is a double-edged gift for small towns.

entries.meaning: Able to bend your fingers, arms or legs much further than most people. ---
examples: She's double-jointed and can bend her thumb to her wrist.
A double-jointed kid in the class could fold herself in half.
Are you double-jointed, or does that just not hurt?
entries.contrast: Nobody really has two joints — it is the everyday word for unusually flexible joints.

entries.meaning: Typed with a full empty line between the lines of text. ---
examples: Papers must be double-spaced and twelve point.
She handed in a double-spaced draft with wide margins.
Is the whole thing double-spaced, including the notes?

entries.meaning: Doubtful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's doubtful that the bill will pass this year.
His return this season looks doubtful.
I'm doubtful about spending that much on a roof.
She sounded more doubtful the second time I asked.

senses.head: Unlikely to happen or to be true
examples: It's doubtful that the bill will pass this year.
His return this season looks doubtful.

senses.head: Not sure that something is right or will work
examples: I'm doubtful about spending that much on a roof.
She sounded more doubtful the second time I asked.

entries.takes: about or of + noun; that- or whether-clause
entries.contrast: The b is silent: DOWT-fuhl. With a thing as subject it means 'unlikely' (It's doubtful that he'll come); with a person it means 'unsure' (I'm doubtful about the plan).

entries.meaning: Showing that you do not believe or trust something. ---
examples: He gave me a doubting look and asked for the receipt.
Even the doubting neighbors showed up to see it.
Don't be such a doubting Thomas.
entries.contrast: A doubting Thomas is someone who won't believe anything until he sees proof.

entries.meaning: Doughy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The middle of the loaf is still doughy.
That pizza came out doughier than the last one.
He looked pale and doughy after a winter indoors.
A doughy man in a gray suit took our names.

senses.head: Soft and undercooked inside, like raw dough
examples: The middle of the loaf is still doughy.
That pizza came out doughier than the last one.

senses.head: Of a face or body: pale, soft and unhealthy-looking
examples: He looked pale and doughy after a winter indoors.
A doughy man in a gray suit took our names.

entries.meaning: Unfriendly and severe, showing no warmth or humor. ---
examples: The dour clerk didn't look up once.
He gets dour when the subject turns to money.
She's the most dour coach in the conference.
entries.contrast: Most Americans say /ˈdaʊər/, to rhyme with hour; /dʊr/ is also heard.

entries.meaning: Favoring peace and talks rather than force, or favoring low interest rates rather than tight money. ---
examples: She took a dovish line on the intervention.
The statement was more dovish than traders expected.
Two dovish members voted against the hike.

entries.meaning: Dressed in dull, old-fashioned clothes. ---
examples: She felt dowdy next to the other guests.
The costume department made her look dowdier than she is.
He described the hotel as comfortable but dowdy.
entries.contrast: It is about dull, old-fashioned clothes, not about being ugly, and it is said almost only about women — so it stings.

entries.meaning: Down has 4 distinct senses.
examples: She's been down since the funeral.
I get a little down in February.
The payment system is down again.
Their site was down for six hours.
Sales are down eight percent this quarter.
Gas prices are down from last summer.
We were down by two with a minute left.
They're down three games to one in the series.

senses.head: Sad or depressed
examples: She's been down since the funeral.
I get a little down in February.

senses.head: Of a computer, network or machine: not working
examples: The payment system is down again.
Their site was down for six hours.

senses.head: Lower in number or amount than before
examples: Sales are down eight percent this quarter.
Gas prices are down from last summer.

senses.head: Losing by a certain amount in a game
examples: We were down by two with a minute left.
They're down three games to one in the series.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: the system is down
entries.comparison: not gradable — really down, way down
entries.contrast: Down is mostly a preposition (down the street), an adverb (sit down), a verb and a noun. Only the meanings below work as adjectives. Note a down payment, where down is not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Learned or practiced so well that you can do it perfectly every time. ---
examples: She has her opening line down pat.
After a week he had the espresso machine down pat.
Get the first ten measures down pat before you go on.
entries.position: predicative only — after have or get + object: I have it down pat
entries.contrast: It follows the object, not the verb be: say She has the routine down pat, never the routine is down pat.

entries.meaning: Having no money, no job and nowhere to live. ---
examples: The diner fed down-and-out regulars for free.
He was down and out the winter after the plant closed.
It's a movie about a down-and-out boxer.
entries.form: compound — the phrase down and out used as one adjective
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a shelter for the down-and-outs. After a verb the hyphens usually drop: He was down and out for a while.

entries.meaning: Practical, sensible and easy to talk to, with no airs. ---
examples: For a famous actor, she's remarkably down-to-earth.
We need a down-to-earth plan, not a wish list.
He's the most down-to-earth person on the board.
entries.form: compound — the phrase down to earth used as one adjective
entries.contrast: In English this is praise — sensible and unpretentious — while Russian приземлённый can sound like an insult.

entries.meaning: Downcast has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She looked downcast when the letter finally came.
A downcast group of fans filed out of the stadium.
He seemed more downcast than angry.
She answered with downcast eyes.
He stood in the doorway, his face downcast.

senses.head: Sad and discouraged
examples: She looked downcast when the letter finally came.
A downcast group of fans filed out of the stadium.
He seemed more downcast than angry.

senses.head: Looking down at the ground
examples: She answered with downcast eyes.
He stood in the doorway, his face downcast.

entries.meaning: Going or sloping down. ---
examples: The last mile of the race is downhill.
She took the downhill trail back to the car.
Downhill skiing is the only sport he follows.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb: We walked downhill for an hour. And in It's all downhill from here it can mean either easier or worse, so the rest of the sentence has to tell you which.

entries.meaning: Meant for people with less money; plain and cheap. ---
examples: They moved to a more downscale part of town.
The chain opened a downscale version of its steakhouses.
The hotel felt downscale next to the one on the river.
entries.form: down + scale, made on the pattern of upscale
entries.contrast: American. Upscale is far more common than downscale.

entries.meaning: On a lower floor of a building. ---
examples: The downstairs bathroom is being painted.
Our downstairs neighbors complained about the noise.
He keeps his tools in the downstairs closet.
entries.contrast: Usually an adverb (She went downstairs). As an adjective it only goes before a noun — never the bathroom is downstairs with this meaning.

entries.meaning: Downstream has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The downstream towns were warned about flooding.
Our camp was downstream from the falls.
Downstream costs were higher than anyone expected.
Refining is the downstream end of the oil business.

senses.head: Farther along a river, in the direction the water flows
examples: The downstream towns were warned about flooding.
Our camp was downstream from the falls.

senses.head: Coming later in a process or a chain of business
examples: Downstream costs were higher than anyone expected.
Refining is the downstream end of the oil business.

entries.meaning: In or belonging to the business center of a city. ---
examples: She works at a downtown law firm.
The downtown stores all close at six.
Downtown traffic is terrible on Fridays.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb and a noun: We drove downtown. American — the British say city centre.

entries.meaning: Treated badly for a long time by people with power, and worn down by it. ---
examples: The novel is about the downtrodden mill workers of the 1930s.
She felt downtrodden after ten years in that job.
Downtrodden tenants finally took the landlord to court.
entries.form: compound — down + the old participle of tread

entries.meaning: Moving or pointing toward a lower level. ---
examples: Sales have been on a downward trend all year.
He made a small downward motion with his hand.
The downward pressure on wages continued into the spring.
entries.contrast: The adverb is downward or downwards: Prices moved downward. The adjective has no -s and goes before the noun.

entries.meaning: In the direction the wind is blowing; on the side the wind carries smells and smoke toward. ---
examples: We stayed downwind of the deer so they wouldn't smell us.
Farms downwind of the plant reported the smell for years.
The downwind side of the island gets far less rain.
entries.position: both — often after a verb: We were downwind of the fire

entries.meaning: Drab has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The office walls were a drab olive green.
Her winter coat was even drabber than mine.
He was tired of his drab little town.
The report makes life on the base sound drab.

senses.head: Dull in color and not pleasant to look at
examples: The office walls were a drab olive green.
Her winter coat was even drabber than mine.

senses.head: Boring and cheerless
examples: He was tired of his drab little town.
The report makes life on the base sound drab.

entries.contrast: Doubles the b in comparison: drabber, not draber.

entries.meaning: Extremely harsh and severe, especially about rules or punishment. ---
examples: The new phone rules struck many parents as draconian.
Critics called the budget cuts draconian.
The school took draconian measures against cheating.
entries.form: from Draco, an Athenian lawgiver famous for harsh punishments

entries.meaning: Letting in currents of cold air. ---
examples: The old farmhouse was drafty in the winter.
We put plastic over the drafty windows.
The upstairs bedroom is even draftier than the living room.
entries.form: -y from draft (a current of cold air)
entries.contrast: American spelling is drafty; British English writes draughty.

entries.meaning: Very tired, with no energy or emotion left. ---
examples: After the funeral, everyone felt completely drained.
She came home from her shift looking drained.
I was more drained by the meeting than by the eight-hour drive.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: I feel drained
entries.form: -ed from drain — how the person feels
entries.contrast: drained is how you feel; draining is what makes you feel that way: The trip was draining, and I was drained.

entries.meaning: Making you feel very tired and without energy. ---
examples: Caring for a sick parent is emotionally draining.
It was a long, draining week at work.
Online classes were more draining than I expected.
entries.form: -ing from drain — what causes the feeling

entries.meaning: Extreme and sudden, with a strong effect. ---
examples: The company took drastic steps to cut costs.
Don't do anything drastic until we talk.
The change in her appearance was more drastic than I'd imagined.

entries.meaning: Looking thin, pale and tired because of worry, illness or pain. ---
examples: His face was drawn after three nights in the hospital.
She looked pale and drawn at the trial.
He seemed more drawn every time I visited.
entries.position: both — mostly after look: She looked pale and drawn
entries.contrast: In I've always been drawn to the ocean (attracted to) and with the curtains drawn (closed), drawn is the verb draw in the passive.

entries.meaning: Lasting longer than necessary or than you want. ---
examples: The divorce was a long, drawn-out process.
Nobody wanted another drawn-out legal battle.
This year's budget talks were even more drawn-out than last year's.
entries.position: both — often long, drawn-out; after a verb usually drawn out: The process was drawn out
entries.form: compound — participle + adverb, from draw out

entries.meaning: Feared or strongly disliked; often used humorously about something unpleasant but ordinary. ---
examples: Then came the dreaded question: "So, when are you getting married?"
My laptop showed the dreaded blue screen.
For many students, the SAT is the most dreaded test of high school.
entries.position: attributive only — usually the dreaded: the dreaded phone call

entries.meaning: Dreadful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The food at the hotel was dreadful.
We heard about the dreadful accident on the news.
It was the most dreadful movie I've ever sat through.
I feel dreadful about forgetting your birthday.
She had the flu and looked dreadful.

senses.head: Very bad or very unpleasant
examples: The food at the hotel was dreadful.
We heard about the dreadful accident on the news.
It was the most dreadful movie I've ever sat through.

senses.head: Feeling ill, or feeling very sorry or guilty about something
examples: I feel dreadful about forgetting your birthday.
She had the flu and looked dreadful.

entries.meaning: Strange, unreal or beautiful, as if happening in a dream. ---
examples: The fog gave the valley a dreamlike quality.
The whole wedding day felt dreamlike.
His later paintings became more dreamlike and abstract.

entries.meaning: Dreamy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She had a dreamy look on her face.
He was a quiet, dreamy kid who loved to read.
The band plays slow, dreamy pop songs.
This cake is even dreamier with whipped cream.
Her new boyfriend is so dreamy.
The actor was voted the dreamiest guy in Hollywood.

senses.head: Thinking about pleasant things and not paying attention to what is happening
examples: She had a dreamy look on her face.
He was a quiet, dreamy kid who loved to read.

senses.head: Soft, gentle and pleasant, like something in a dream
examples: The band plays slow, dreamy pop songs.
This cake is even dreamier with whipped cream.

senses.head: Informal: very attractive
examples: Her new boyfriend is so dreamy.
The actor was voted the dreamiest guy in Hollywood.

entries.meaning: Dull, gray and depressing. ---
examples: It was a cold, dreary day in February.
The office was dreary, with no windows at all.
His second novel is even drearier than his first.

entries.meaning: Completely wet. ---
examples: We got caught in the storm and came home drenched.
His shirt was drenched in sweat.
She pulled off her drenched socks.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: We got drenched
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with completely, totally: totally drenched
entries.takes: in or with + noun: drenched in sweat, drenched with rain
entries.form: -ed from drench; also in compounds: sun-drenched

entries.meaning: Dressed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Hurry up and get dressed — the bus is coming.
I'm not dressed yet, so don't open the door.
He was fully dressed by six in the morning.
She was dressed in a long blue coat.
The kids were dressed as superheroes for Halloween.
He's always well dressed for meetings.

senses.head: Wearing clothes, not naked or in pajamas
examples: Hurry up and get dressed — the bus is coming.
I'm not dressed yet, so don't open the door.
He was fully dressed by six in the morning.

senses.head: Wearing a particular kind or style of clothes
examples: She was dressed in a long blue coat.
The kids were dressed as superheroes for Halloween.
He's always well dressed for meetings.

entries.position: both — alone after a verb: get dressed; before a noun with an adverb: a well-dressed man
entries.comparison: not gradable — but better dressed, best-dressed with well
entries.takes: in + clothes or color: dressed in black; as + character: dressed as a pirate; for + occasion: dressed for work
entries.contrast: Russian says одеваться, but English says get dressed, not dress myself in everyday speech. dressed up means wearing formal or special clothes: Why are you all dressed up?

entries.meaning: Of clothes or an event: formal and elegant, not casual. ---
examples: Is the party dressy, or can I wear jeans?
She bought a dressy black jacket for the wedding.
You'll need something dressier than that sweater.

entries.meaning: With the water removed so that it keeps for a long time. ---
examples: Add a cup of dried cranberries to the salad.
The recipe calls for dried beans, not canned ones.
She hung bunches of dried flowers in the kitchen.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb English usually says dry: The paint is dry

entries.meaning: With all the water gone; no longer wet, fresh or full of life. ---
examples: We walked along a dried-up riverbed.
The flowers on the table were brown and dried-up.
All that was left of the lake was a dried-up patch of mud.
entries.position: both — after a verb usually dried up: The creek is dried up
entries.form: compound — participle + adverb, from dry up

entries.meaning: Drinkable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Is the tap water drinkable here?
The filter makes stream water drinkable.
It's a cheap but very drinkable red wine.
The coffee got more drinkable after I added milk.

senses.head: Clean and safe enough to drink
examples: Is the tap water drinkable here?
The filter makes stream water drinkable.

senses.head: Of wine, beer or coffee: pleasant and easy to drink
examples: It's a cheap but very drinkable red wine.
The coffee got more drinkable after I added milk.

entries.meaning: Extremely determined to succeed and working very hard. ---
examples: She's a driven young lawyer who works seventy hours a week.
Even as a teenager, he was incredibly driven.
My sister was always more driven than I was.
entries.form: past participle of drive; also a suffix: data-driven, market-driven

entries.meaning: Driving has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We changed the tire in driving rain.
The hikers turned back in the driving snow.
She was the driving force behind the project.
Fear of losing customers was the driving factor in the decision.

senses.head: Of rain or snow: falling very hard and blown by the wind
examples: We changed the tire in driving rain.
The hikers turned back in the driving snow.

senses.head: Having a strong influence that makes something happen
examples: She was the driving force behind the project.
Fear of losing customers was the driving factor in the decision.

entries.contrast: In driving lessons and a driving test, driving is a noun (the activity of driving a car) used as a modifier, not this adjective.

entries.meaning: With light, fine rain falling. ---
examples: It was a gray, drizzly morning in Seattle.
The weather stayed drizzly all weekend.
The coast is usually more drizzly than the valley.

entries.meaning: Funny in a quiet, clever or unusual way. ---
examples: He has a droll sense of humor.
"Well, that went well," she said in a droll voice.
Her essays are more droll than laugh-out-loud funny.
entries.contrast: droll is quiet, dry, clever humor — not loud or silly. It is a bookish word; everyday speech says funny or dry.

entries.meaning: Hanging down, often because of being weak or tired. ---
examples: The basset hound has long, droopy ears.
My plants get droopy if I forget to water them.
His eyelids got droopier as the lecture went on.

entries.meaning: Tired and almost asleep. ---
examples: This medicine may make you drowsy.
Don't drive if you feel drowsy.

Physical therapy is a drug-free way to manage back pain.

examples: The sign said "Drug-Free School Zone."
He has been drug-free for five years.

senses.head: Done without using medicine
examples: She wanted a drug-free birth.
Physical therapy is a drug-free way to manage back pain.

Police believe the victim was given a drugged drink.
The guard fell asleep after eating the drugged sandwich.

senses.head: Sleepy or confused because of a drug
examples: After the surgery, he was still drugged and couldn't talk.
She woke up feeling drugged and heavy.

senses.head: Of food or drink: with a drug secretly added

The guard fell asleep after eating the drugged sandwich.

entries.meaning: Drunk has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He got drunk at his brother's wedding.
A drunk driver ran the red light.
She was drunker than anyone else at the party.
The new manager was drunk with power.
They were drunk on their early success.

senses.head: Having had so much alcohol that you cannot think or act normally
examples: He got drunk at his brother's wedding.
A drunk driver ran the red light.
She was drunker than anyone else at the party.

senses.head: So excited by a feeling that you do not act sensibly
examples: The new manager was drunk with power.
They were drunk on their early success.

entries.position: both — He was drunk; a drunk driver
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — drunker, drunkest, more drunk
entries.takes: on + drink: drunk on cheap wine; with or on + feeling: drunk with power
entries.contrast: drunken also means 'drunk' but goes only before a noun and often describes behavior: a drunken fight. a drunk is a noun, 'a person who is often drunk'. The verb forms are drink, drank, drunk: I have drunk, not I have drank.

entries.meaning: Having two parts, uses or roles. ---
examples: She holds dual citizenship in the US and Canada.
The room serves a dual purpose as an office and a guest room.
The car has dual airbags in the front.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like duel, 'a fight between two people'.

They won the dubious honor of being the worst team in the league.

senses.head: Not sure that something is good or true

senses.head: Boring and not interesting
examples: The lecture was long and dull.
Life in a small town can be dull.
This is the dullest book I've ever read.

examples: The paint had faded to a dull green.
It was a dull, overcast afternoon.

senses.head: Of a blade: not sharp
examples: Be careful — a dull knife slips more easily.
These scissors are getting duller every week.

senses.head: Of a pain or sound: not strong or clear
examples: I have a dull ache in my lower back.

entries.meaning: Dumb has 2 distinct senses.

She stood there dumb with amazement.

senses.head: Informal: stupid
examples: That was a really dumb mistake.
Don't ask dumb questions.
It's the dumbest movie I've seen all year.

senses.head: For a short time unable to speak because of shock or surprise
examples: We were struck dumb by the news.
She stood there dumb with amazement.

entries.contrast: The b is silent. In everyday American English dumb means 'stupid'. The old meaning 'unable to speak' is offensive about people; say nonspeaking or unable to speak. It survives in struck dumb.

entries.meaning: So surprised that you cannot speak. ---
examples: I was completely dumbfounded by her answer.

The fans sat in dumbfounded silence after the loss.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: I was dumbfounded
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with completely, absolutely

entries.meaning: So shocked or amazed that you cannot speak. ---
examples: The audience was dumbstruck by the ending.
He stood dumbstruck in the doorway.
She gave me a dumbstruck look.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: She was dumbstruck

entries.meaning: Dumpy has 2 distinct senses.

We stayed in a dumpy motel off the highway.

senses.head: Of a person or thing: short and fat; not a kind word
examples: The character was a dumpy little man in a brown suit.
She felt dumpy in the oversized sweater.

senses.head: Informal, of a place: dirty, old and in bad condition
examples: We stayed in a dumpy motel off the highway.
Their first apartment was even dumpier than this one.

entries.meaning: Exactly the same as something else; made as a copy. ---

The system found two duplicate files.
Please don't send duplicate payments.
entries.contrast: The adjective and noun end in /kət/; the verb to duplicate ends in /keɪt/: a DOO-pli-kuht key, but don't DOO-pli-kayt the work.

entries.meaning: Dishonest; saying one thing and secretly doing another. ---
examples: The senator was accused of being duplicitous.

The villain in the second season is even more duplicitous.

Washing machines and furniture count as durable goods.

senses.head: Staying in good condition or lasting for a long time
examples: These boots are made of durable leather.
Plastic plates are more durable than glass ones.
Both sides hoped for a durable peace.

senses.head: In economics, of goods: expected to be used for several years, like cars and refrigerators
examples: Orders for durable goods fell last month.
Washing machines and furniture count as durable goods.

The roads get dusty in August.

senses.head: Of a color: soft and slightly gray
examples: The bridesmaids wore dusty pink.

entries.meaning: Doing what you should do or what others expect, often without enthusiasm. ---

entries.meaning: Sold without government import taxes. ---

senses.head: About to die

senses.head: Disappearing or coming to an end
